subsection: 4. Landforms associated with particular rock types

notes.b: Karst is a landscape on limestone shaped mainly by solution, with few surface streams and many underground features. The name comes from the Kras plateau of Slovenia.
points: Limestone is calcium carbonate. Carbonation: rainwater containing carbon dioxide forms weak carbonic acid, which reacts with the rock to form soluble calcium bicarbonate: CaCO3 + H2O + CO2 gives Ca(HCO3)2.
Permeable rock lets water pass through it, mainly along cracks. Porous rock has tiny spaces between its grains that can hold water. Impermeable rock lets no water pass through.
Limestone is permeable because water moves along its bedding planes (horizontal layers) and joints (vertical cracks), not through the solid rock.
The ground water table is the upper surface of the zone where all cracks in the rock are saturated. Above it lies the zone of aeration. It rises in wet weather and falls in dry weather.
Percolation is the downward movement of water through soil and rock.

notes.b: Limestone pavement is a bare, flat limestone surface, exposed when glacial ice scraped away the soil.
points: Stage 1: ice removes the soil cover, exposing the jointed and bedded rock to rain.
Stage 2: carbonation widens the joints into grikes.
Stage 3: the blocks left standing between the grikes are clints.
Grikes: deep, narrow vertical cracks widened by carbonation along joints.
Clints: flat-topped blocks of limestone between grikes.
Karren (runnels): small grooves cut into clint surfaces by rainwater running across them.
Solution hollows (kamenitza or solution pans): small enclosed hollows on clint surfaces where rainwater collects and dissolves the rock.
Burren, Co. Clare: Ireland's best-known karst landscape, of Carboniferous limestone with extensive pavement of clints and grikes. Its name comes from the Irish 'Boireann', meaning rocky place.
Diagram: plan of clints and grikes; cross-section showing bedding planes and joints in the rock.

notes.h: Swallow holes, dolines, poljes and turloughs
points: Swallow hole (slugga): a surface stream flowing off impermeable rock reaches limestone and disappears underground down a hole widened by carbonation along a joint.
Doline (sinkhole): a hollow formed by solution of the surface, or by collapse of a cave roof. A doline formed by cave collapse is still a doline.
Uvala: several dolines merged into one larger hollow.
Polje: a large, flat-floored depression that floods seasonally. Poljes occur in Slovenia.
Dry valley: a valley cut by a surface river when the ground was frozen (and so impermeable) or the water table was higher. It now carries no stream.
Turlough: a seasonal lake in a hollow in limestone. It fills in winter when the water table rises and drains through the floor in summer.
Turloughs are common in the Burren and east Co. Galway. Rahasane turlough, near Craughwell, Co. Galway, is one of the largest.

River of resurgence: an underground river that re-emerges at the surface, usually where limestone meets impermeable rock below. It is the reverse of a swallow hole, which takes a surface stream underground.
Diagram: cross-section from impermeable rock, through a swallow hole, underground to the resurgence.
Caves and caverns: water dissolves passages along bedding planes and joints, and underground rivers enlarge them by erosion. A cavern is a very large cave.
Examples: Aillwee Cave, Co. Clare (Burren); Mitchelstown Cave, Co. Tipperary.
Dripstone formation: water dripping from the roof carries dissolved calcium bicarbonate. When it loses carbon dioxide and evaporates, it deposits calcite (calcium carbonate).
Stalactites hang from the roof and grow downward. Stalactite: C for ceiling.
Stalagmites grow upward from the floor beneath and are usually thicker and blunter. Stalagmite: G for ground.
Pillars (columns) form where a stalactite and a stalagmite join.
Curtains are sheets of calcite formed where water trickles along a crack in the roof.
Doolin Cave, Co. Clare, holds the Great Stalactite, about 7.3 m long, one of the longest free-hanging stalactites in the world.
Diagram: labelled cross-section of a cave showing stalactites, stalagmites, a pillar, a swallow hole and an underground river.

notes.b: A karst landscape develops through three stages.
points: Youth: surface drainage begins to sink, and swallow holes form.
Maturity: most drainage goes underground, with caves, dolines and uvalas.
Old age: cave roofs collapse, the limestone is mostly removed, and isolated residual hills remain.

notes.h: Karst settings in Ireland and abroad
points: Marble Arch upland: the Marble Arch Caves lie on the slopes of Cuilcagh Mountain, Co. Fermanagh. They are part of the cross-border Marble Arch Caves Global Geopark with Co. Cavan.
Streams flowing off the impermeable shale and sandstone of Cuilcagh sink into swallow holes where they reach the limestone, flow through the caves and re-emerge as the Cladagh River.
The Marble Arch is a natural limestone arch over the Cladagh. The Shannon Pot, the source of the River Shannon, is on the slopes of Cuilcagh in Co. Cavan.
Mask–Corrib lowland: water from Lough Mask flows underground through the limestone to Lough Corrib near Cong, Co. Mayo.
The Cong Canal, built in the mid-1800s to link the two lakes, never held water because it leaked into the permeable limestone. It became known as the dry canal.
Slovenia: Postojna Cave and the Škocjan Caves, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Poljes occur here.
South-west China: Guilin and the Li River have tower karst, steep-sided limestone hills. The South China Karst is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Kentucky, USA: Mammoth Cave is the longest known cave system in the world.
Jamaica: Cockpit Country has cockpit karst, steep conical hills separated by deep, star-shaped hollows.

notes.h: Granite landscapes: rock properties and Wicklow
notes.b: Granite is hard, crystalline and resistant to erosion, and its landscapes reflect how it drains and weathers.
points: Granite is impermeable: water runs off it, so it has many surface streams and boggy ground.
Granite is jointed. It weathers mainly by hydrolysis of its feldspar, which forms clay.
China clay (kaolin) is the clay that results. It is quarried at Lee Moor, on the south-west edge of Dartmoor.
The Leinster batholith, the largest granite mass in Ireland and Britain, forms the Wicklow Mountains.
Its rounded, dome-shaped uplands are worn down from rock that once covered the granite.
Impermeable granite with high rainfall gives thin, acidic soils and blanket bog, e.g. on the Sally Gap area of Co. Wicklow.
Ice cut deep valleys into the granite (see the notes on Glacial processes, patterns and associated landforms (Glaciation)).
Tor: a block of granite standing on a hilltop.

Two-stage formation, put forward by D. L. Linton in 1955. Stage 1: under warm, wet conditions, deep chemical weathering (hydrolysis) attacked the granite along its joints, rotting it most where the joints were closest together.
Stage 2: the rotted material was later stripped away, e.g. by mass movement under periglacial conditions, leaving solid, widely jointed blocks standing as tors.
An alternative theory explains tors by freeze-thaw and solifluction alone.
Clitter: blockfields of boulders on the slopes below tors.
Dartmoor, Devon, England: a granite upland with tors such as Haytor and Hound Tor, clitter on its slopes and blanket bog.
Diagram: cross-section showing the rotted zone along joints and the standing tor after stripping.

notes.h: Spatial variation in rock type and the physical landscape
points: Ireland's saucer shape: a low central lowland of Carboniferous limestone is ringed by uplands of harder, more resistant rocks such as granite, quartzite and sandstone.
Differential erosion: resistant rock forms uplands, headlands and peaks, while weaker rock forms lowlands, valleys and bays.
Quartzite peaks stand above the surrounding rock: Errigal, Co. Donegal; Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo; the Great Sugar Loaf, Co. Wicklow.
Rock type and drainage: impermeable granite and shale give many surface streams and bog. Permeable limestone takes drainage underground, leaving few rivers and dry surfaces.
Lough Corrib roughly divides the limestone lowland of east Co. Galway from the granite and metamorphic uplands of Connemara to the west.

keyTerms.definition: A landscape on limestone shaped mainly by solution, with few surface streams and many underground features.
Solution of calcium carbonate by rainwater containing carbon dioxide, forming soluble calcium bicarbonate.
Rock that lets water pass through it, mainly along bedding planes, joints and other cracks.
The upper surface of the zone where all cracks in the rock are saturated with water.
A flat-topped block of limestone between grikes on a limestone pavement.
A deep, narrow vertical crack in limestone pavement, widened by carbonation along joints.
A hole where a surface stream disappears underground into limestone, widened by carbonation along a joint.
A hollow formed by solution of the surface or by collapse of a cave roof.
A seasonal lake in a limestone hollow that fills in winter when the water table rises and drains in summer.
An underground river that re-emerges at the surface, usually where limestone meets impermeable rock below.
A calcite icicle-shaped deposit that hangs from a cave roof and grows downward.
A calcite deposit that grows upward from a cave floor beneath a stalactite.
A block of granite standing on a hilltop, left when the rotted rock around it has been stripped away.
A blockfield of granite boulders on slopes below a tor.
Chemical weathering in which water reacts with minerals such as feldspar, forming clay.

factCards.term: Limestone: two reasons it develops karst landforms
factCards.definition: It is calcium carbonate, which dissolves in weak carbonic acid by carbonation. It is permeable: water passes along its bedding planes (horizontal) and joints (vertical), not through the solid rock, so drainage goes underground.

factCards.term: Permeable, porous and impermeable rock: the difference
factCards.definition: Permeable rock lets water pass through it, mainly along cracks such as joints and bedding planes. Porous rock holds water in tiny spaces between its grains. Impermeable rock lets no water pass through.

factCards.term: Limestone pavement: how it forms, in stages
factCards.definition: First, glacial ice scrapes away the soil, exposing the jointed, bedded limestone to rain; then carbonation widens the joints into grikes; the blocks left standing between them are clints. Example: the Burren, Co. Clare.

factCards.term: Limestone pavement: how karren and solution hollows form on clints
factCards.definition: Karren (runnels) are small grooves cut into clint surfaces by rainwater running across them. Solution hollows (kamenitza) are small enclosed hollows where rainwater collects on a clint and dissolves the rock.

factCards.term: The Burren: key facts for a karst answer
factCards.definition: Ireland's best-known karst landscape, in Co. Clare, of Carboniferous limestone with extensive pavement of clints and grikes. Its name comes from the Irish Boireann, meaning rocky place. Mullaghmore is a Burren hill of folded, terraced limestone.

factCards.term: Swallow hole to river of resurgence: what happens to a stream
factCards.definition: A stream flowing off impermeable rock reaches limestone and sinks down a swallow hole widened by carbonation along a joint; it flows underground through caves and re-emerges as a river of resurgence, usually where limestone meets impermeable rock below.

factCards.term: Turlough: how it fills and empties, with an Irish example
factCards.definition: In winter the water table rises and floods a hollow in the limestone, forming a seasonal lake; in summer it drains away through the floor. Turloughs are common in the Burren and east Co. Galway; Rahasane, near Craughwell, is one of the largest.

factCards.term: Doline, uvala, polje and dry valley: what each is
factCards.definition: Doline: a hollow formed by solution of the surface or collapse of a cave roof. Uvala: several merged dolines. Polje: a large, flat-floored, seasonally flooded depression (Slovenia). Dry valley: cut by a river when the ground was frozen or water table higher.

factCards.term: Stalactites, stalagmites and pillars: how they form
factCards.definition: Water dripping from a cave roof carries dissolved calcium bicarbonate; as it loses carbon dioxide and evaporates it deposits calcite. Stalactites grow down from the roof, stalagmites up from the floor beneath, and a pillar forms where the two join.

factCards.term: Caves: how they form, with three Irish examples
factCards.definition: Water dissolves passages along bedding planes and joints, and underground rivers enlarge them by erosion. Examples: Aillwee Cave, Co. Clare; Doolin Cave, Co. Clare, with the Great Stalactite, about 7.3 m long; Mitchelstown Cave, Co. Tipperary.

factCards.term: Karst cycle: the three stages
factCards.definition: Youth: surface drainage begins to sink and swallow holes form. Maturity: most drainage goes underground, with caves, dolines and uvalas. Old age: cave roofs collapse, the limestone is mostly removed and isolated residual hills remain.

factCards.term: Marble Arch upland: how its drainage works
factCards.definition: On Cuilcagh Mountain, Co. Fermanagh, streams flow off impermeable shale and sandstone and sink into swallow holes at the limestone, flow through the Marble Arch Caves and re-emerge as the Cladagh River; the Marble Arch is a natural limestone arch over it.

factCards.term: Mask–Corrib lowland: two signs of underground karst drainage
factCards.definition: Water from Lough Mask flows underground through the limestone to Lough Corrib near Cong, Co. Mayo. The Cong Canal, built in the mid-1800s to link the two lakes, never held water because it leaked into the permeable limestone: the dry canal.

factCards.term: Name four international karst areas and a feature of each
factCards.definition: Slovenia: the Kras plateau, which gives karst its name, with Postojna Cave and the Škocjan Caves. S.W. China: tower karst at Guilin and the Li River. Kentucky: Mammoth Cave, the world's longest known cave system. Jamaica: cockpit karst in Cockpit Country.

factCards.term: Granite landscapes: four characteristics of granite that shape them
factCards.definition: Hard, crystalline and resistant to erosion; impermeable, so water runs off, giving many surface streams and boggy ground; jointed; weathers mainly by hydrolysis of its feldspar, which forms clay (china clay).

factCards.term: Wicklow granite landscape: its main features
factCards.definition: The Leinster batholith, the largest granite mass in Ireland and Britain, forms rounded, dome-shaped uplands, worn down from rock that once covered it; impermeable rock and high rainfall give thin, acidic soils and blanket bog, e.g. around the Sally Gap.

factCards.term: Tors: the two-stage (deep weathering) theory of formation
factCards.definition: First, under warm, wet conditions, hydrolysis rotted the granite deep along its joints, most where they were close together; later, mass movement under periglacial conditions stripped the rotted rock, leaving widely jointed blocks as tors (D. L. Linton, 1955).

factCards.term: Dartmoor: four granite landscape features with examples
factCards.definition: A granite upland in Devon, England, with tors such as Haytor and Hound Tor, clitter (boulder fields) on the slopes below them, blanket bog, and china clay quarried at Lee Moor on its south-west edge.

factCards.term: Rock type and the Irish landscape: saucer shape and quartzite peaks
factCards.definition: A low central lowland of Carboniferous limestone is ringed by uplands of harder rock (granite, quartzite, sandstone). By differential erosion, resistant rock forms uplands and peaks, e.g. the quartzite peaks of Errigal, Croagh Patrick and the Great Sugar Loaf.

factCards.term: Two contrasting landscapes either side of Lough Corrib
factCards.definition: East of Lough Corrib lies the limestone lowland of east Co. Galway, with underground drainage, few rivers and dry surfaces; to the west lie the granite and metamorphic uplands of Connemara, with many surface streams and bog.

questions.prompt: Examine the formation of one surface feature and one underground feature of a karst landscape.
questions.model: Surface feature: limestone pavement. Ice removed the soil cover, exposing the jointed limestone to rain. Carbonation widened the joints into grikes, leaving flat-topped clints between them. Rainwater running across the clints cut karren, and rainwater pooling in hollows dissolved solution hollows. The Burren, Co. Clare, is the best-known example. Diagram: plan of clints and grikes, with a cross-section showing bedding planes and joints. Underground feature: stalactites, stalagmites and pillars. Water passes along bedding planes and joints and dissolves passages, which underground rivers enlarge into caves. Dripwater from the roof carries dissolved calcium bicarbonate. When it loses carbon dioxide and evaporates, it deposits calcite. Stalactites hang from the roof and grow downward; stalagmites grow upward from the floor, usually thicker and blunter; a pillar forms where they join. Example: Doolin Cave, Co. Clare, with the Great Stalactite of about 7.3 m. Diagram: labelled cave cross-section showing a stalactite, a stalagmite and a pillar.

questions.prompt: Explain how spatial variations in rock type influence the physical landscape, with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Limestone is permeable, so water drains underground through bedding planes and joints. The Burren and the Marble Arch upland have karst landscapes with few surface streams, swallow holes and caves. In the Mask-Corrib lowland, water flows underground from Lough Mask to Lough Corrib, and the Cong Canal never held water. Granite is resistant and impermeable. In the Wicklow granite, rounded uplands, thin acidic soils, blanket bog and many surface streams result. On Dartmoor, tors and clitter stand above the granite slopes. Quartzite is resistant, so quartzite peaks such as Errigal and Croagh Patrick stand above the surrounding rocks. Resistant rock forms uplands and peaks; weaker limestone forms the central lowland of Ireland's saucer shape.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the terms permeable rock and ground water table.
questions.model: Permeable rock lets water pass through it, mainly along cracks, joints and bedding planes; limestone is an example. The ground water table is the upper surface of the zone where all cracks in the rock are saturated with water. Above it lies the zone of aeration. It rises in wet weather and falls in dry weather.
